lessons.title: How to conduct a client meeting in person or via WhatsApp call
lessons.body: Start by scheduling the meeting at a time that works for both of you. If in person, choose a neutral place like a cafÃ© or your office. If via WhatsApp call, confirm the time and ensure you have a stable internet connection. Before the call, prepare a notebook and pen, and have a simple questionnaire ready with key questions about the event. Begin the meeting by introducing yourself and your business. Be friendly and professional. Ask open-ended questions to understand their vision. For example, 'Tell me about the event you are planning.' Listen more than you talk. Take notes on important details like date, venue, guest count, and budget. If on WhatsApp, you can ask them to send pictures or voice notes for clarity. After the meeting, summarize what you discussed and send a follow-up message thanking them. This shows you are organized and serious. Always confirm the next steps, like sending a quote or visiting the venue. Remember, a good consultation builds trust and helps you avoid costly mistakes later.

lessons.title: Asking the right questions: guest count, budget, date, and cultural requirements
lessons.body: The success of any event depends on asking the right questions. Start with the date and time. Is it flexible? Check if it clashes with other events. Next, ask about the guest count. This affects everything from seating to catering. Get an exact number or a range. Then, discuss the budget. Be direct: 'What is your budget for decor and planning?' If they are unsure, give a range based on similar events. For example, a simple decor for 50 guests might cost between $500 and $1000. Cultural requirements are crucial in Africa. Ask about traditions, colors, and any specific rituals. For instance, in many African weddings, certain colors are symbolic. Also, ask about dietary restrictions and religious practices. Other important questions: venue (indoor or outdoor), theme, and must-have items. Write down all answers. If the client is unsure, offer suggestions based on your experience. Always confirm the answers to avoid misunderstandings. After the meeting, compile the information into a brief. This will guide your planning and quoting. Remember, thorough questioning saves time and money.

lessons.title: Creating a simple event brief template using pen and paper
lessons.body: An event brief is a summary of all the key details. You don't need a computer; pen and paper work perfectly. Start with a blank sheet. At the top, write 'Event Brief' and the date. Then, create sections. Section 1: Client details â name, phone, email. Section 2: Event details â type (wedding, birthday), date, time, venue. Section 3: Guest count â number of guests, VIPs. Section 4: Budget â total budget and breakdown if possible. Section 5: Decor requirements â colors, theme, specific items (e.g., 10 centerpieces, backdrop). Section 6: Cultural or special requests â traditions, rituals. Section 7: Timeline â key deadlines. Section 8: Notes â any other important information. Leave space at the bottom for both you and the client to sign and date. This makes it a simple agreement. Keep the brief concise, one or two pages. Use a ruler to draw lines for neatness. After filling it, read it back to the client to confirm accuracy. Then, make two copies: one for you, one for the client. This simple document prevents disputes and ensures you both are on the same page.

lessons.title: Managing client expectations for outdoor and indoor events
lessons.body: Outdoor events in Africa come with unique challenges: weather, insects, and power supply. Be upfront with clients about these. For example, if it's rainy season, suggest a tent or an indoor backup. Explain that wind can affect decor like balloons and drapes. For indoor events, discuss space limitations, ceiling height, and power outlets. Always have a plan B. For outdoor, that might mean renting a generator or having extra tarps. For indoor, check if you can hang decorations without damaging walls. Discuss setup and breakdown times. If the venue has strict rules, inform the client early. Also, talk about guest comfort: shade, seating, and access to toilets. Use real numbers: a 10x10 meter tent can cost around $300 in many African cities. Be honest about what is possible within their budget. If they want a lavish outdoor wedding but have a small budget, suggest alternatives like focusing on a few key decor items. Document all agreed expectations in the brief. This way, if something goes wrong, you have a record. Remember, under-promise and over-deliver.

lessons.title: Handling difficult clients and negotiating changes politely
lessons.body: Difficult clients can be demanding, indecisive, or rude. Stay calm and professional. Listen to their concerns without interrupting. Repeat back what they said to show you understand. For example, 'So you're saying the color scheme is not what you wanted?' Then, offer solutions. If they want changes after the brief is signed, explain that changes may affect cost and timeline. Use polite language: 'I can do that, but it will add $200 to the budget. Would you like to proceed?' If they push back, offer alternatives. For instance, if they want more flowers but have a fixed budget, suggest using cheaper flowers or reducing the number. Never argue. If a client becomes abusive, politely end the conversation and suggest continuing later. Always document changes in writing, even via WhatsApp. Get their confirmation. For negotiations, know your bottom line. Don't agree to work at a loss. If you can't meet their demands, it's okay to decline. Remember, your reputation is important. A difficult client can become a loyal one if you handle them well. Stay patient and focused on finding a win-win solution.

lessons.title: Confirming bookings with a written agreement or deposit receipt
lessons.body: Once the client agrees to your quote, confirm the booking in writing. A simple agreement or deposit receipt is enough. The agreement should include: your business name and contact, client name and contact, event date and venue, services to be provided, total cost, deposit amount, and balance due date. Also, include a cancellation policy. For example, 'Deposit is non-refundable if cancelled within 7 days of event.' Write it clearly, in duplicate. Both parties sign and date. Give one copy to the client. If the client pays a deposit, issue a receipt immediately. The receipt should show the amount paid, date, and remaining balance. You can buy a receipt book from any stationery shop for a few dollars. Always keep a copy for your records. In Africa, many deals are done verbally, but a written agreement protects you. It also makes you look professional. If the client is far, you can send the agreement via WhatsApp and ask them to reply 'I agree' and send a screenshot of the signed copy. For deposits, mobile money is common. Always confirm receipt and send a digital receipt if possible. This step secures your income and reduces no-shows.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Client Consultation and Event Briefing

In the African event services business â weddings, funerals, church conferences, corporate launches, political rallies, and traditional ceremonies â the consultation is where profit is either protected or lost. A decorator in Kampala who takes a brief verbally on WhatsApp and later discovers the client wanted 400 guests instead of 150 has already lost money on fabric, transport, and labour. This reference lesson gives you the exact scripts, templates, and safeguards to run a professional consultation, write a brief that both parties sign, and collect a deposit that holds the date.

Treat every consultation as a business meeting with a measurable output: a written event brief, an agreed budget range, and a deposit receipt. Nothing else counts as a booking.

1. Running the Meeting â In Person or on WhatsApp Call

Most African event clients will first contact you on WhatsApp. That is normal and it is fine â but a WhatsApp text chat is not a consultation. Convert it to a scheduled call or an in-person meeting within 24 hours.

In-person meeting (best for budgets above your local median event spend): Meet at your office, a cafÃ©, or the venue itself if it is a site visit. Bring a notebook, a pen, a tape measure, and your phone for photos. Site visits are the single highest-value consultation you can do â you will spot the mud, the slope, the lack of power, and the distance from the parking area that a client will never mention.

WhatsApp call (good for diaspora clients and distant clients): Confirm the call in writing first. Send a short message: "Good morning Mrs. Achieng. Confirming our consultation call today at 4:00 PM EAT. I will call you on this number. Please have your guest estimate, date, venue name, and budget range ready. The call will take 30 minutes." This one message raises your close rate because it signals professionalism and gives the client time to prepare honest numbers.

During the call, take notes on paper or in a notes app. Repeat every number back to the client before you hang up. Send a WhatsApp summary within two hours: "As discussed: 250 guests, 14 December 2024, Garden Venue, Karen. Budget range KES 180,000â220,000. Deposit KES 60,000 to confirm. Full brief to follow."

2. The Right Questions to Ask

Ask these in order. Do not skip. Write the answers down as the client speaks.

Table 1: Core consultation questions and why they matter
QuestionWhat you are really checkingAfrica-specific note
How many guests are you expecting â confirmed and maximum?Seating, catering, tent size, toilet hireAfrican weddings often grow by 30â50% after invitations. Always plan for the maximum figure.
What is your total budget, and how much is already available?Whether the job is viable and where to cutMany clients quote a "wish budget." Ask for the "must-spend" figure separately.
What is the date, start time, and is there a rain date?Availability and deposit urgencyDecember and Easter are peak. Deposit locks the date; a verbal hold does not.
Is the venue indoor, outdoor, or both?Power, flooring, shade, weather riskOutdoor events in West and East Africa need a rain contingency plan and a mud walkway.
Are there cultural, religious, or family protocol requirements?Colour restrictions, seating hierarchy, ceremony timingExamples: no white at Ghanaian funerals, separate seating at some Muslim weddings, elders seated first at many East African ceremonies.
Who is the final decision-maker?Prevents changes from relatives who are not payingGet the payer's name and number in writing at the first meeting.

Source: Adapted from the client intake framework in The Event Manager's Bible by Des Conway (How To Books), and the pricing and guest-count guidance published by the Kenya Association of Hotelkeepers and Caterers (KAHC) event services guidelines.

3. Creating a Simple Event Brief Template (Pen and Paper)

You do not need software. A single A4 page, written by hand in front of the client, is more powerful than a printed form because the client sees you listening. Use this structure:

  1. Header: Client name, phone, email, date of consultation, your name.
  2. Event details: Type, date, start time, end time, venue name and address.
  3. Guest numbers: Confirmed, maximum, children, VIPs.
  4. Budget: Total, deposit amount, balance due date, payment method.
  5. Scope of work: Exactly what you will deliver â e.g., "Draping for 12 tables, head table backdrop, entrance arch, aisle runner."
  6. Exclusions: What you will NOT do â e.g., "Chair hire, catering, lighting, generator."
  7. Cultural requirements: Colours, seating, ceremony timing, restrictions.
  8. Change policy: "Changes after signing are charged at 15% of the changed item, and must be confirmed in writing 14 days before the event."
  9. Signatures: Client and service provider, with date.

Photograph the signed page and send it to the client on WhatsApp immediately. Keep the original in a physical file. Paper survives power cuts and lost phones.

4. Managing Expectations â Outdoor vs Indoor

Table 2: Risk and cost differences â indoor vs outdoor events
FactorIndoor eventOutdoor eventAction
Weather riskLowHigh (rain, wind, dust, heat)Quote a tent or canopy as standard, not optional.
PowerUsually availableOften noneBudget for generator hire and fuel.
FlooringExistingMud, grass, uneven groundAdd walkway boards or carpet; charge separately.
Set-up time2â4 hours4â8 hoursCharge for extra labour hours.
Toilets and waterExistingMust be hiredClient hires, or you quote it as an add-on.
PermitsRarely neededOften required (county, municipal)Client obtains; put it in the brief as a client responsibility.

Source: Risk categories compiled from the ILO's Safety and Health in the Events and Entertainment Sector guidance and the South African Event Safety Council (SAC) outdoor event planning checklists.

Say this to every outdoor client, word for word: "Madam, I will plan for the weather you want, but I will quote for the weather we may get. If it rains, the tent keeps the event alive. If it does not rain, you have paid for peace of mind. I will not remove the tent from the quote to make the price cheaper, because if it rains I will be blamed."

â  SAFETY WARNING â Outdoor Events

Never erect a tent, stage, or truss on soft ground without anchoring it to stakes or weights rated for wind. In many parts of Africa, afternoon storms arrive within 20 minutes with strong gusts. Collapsed tents and falling trusses have killed and injured guests at weddings and church events. Also: never run generator cables through standing water, and never allow cooking fires or braziers inside or under a tent. If the venue has no safe power source, refuse the job or hire a licensed electrician â do not improvise with domestic extension cables.

5. Handling Difficult Clients and Negotiating Changes Politely

Difficult clients are usually scared clients. They are afraid the event will fail, the family will criticise them, or the money will run out. Your job is to reduce their fear with written clarity, not to win the argument.

The three-step method:

  1. Acknowledge: "I hear you. You want the entrance to look like the photo you sent."
  2. Explain the cost or risk: "That design needs 20 extra metres of fabric and four more hours of labour. That adds KES 18,000."
  3. Offer two options: "Option A: we do the full design and the budget rises. Option B: we keep the budget and use a simpler design that still looks beautiful. Which do you prefer?"

Never say "no." Always say "yes, and here is what it costs." Put every agreed change in a WhatsApp message and ask the client to reply "Confirmed." That reply is your evidence.

For the client who refuses to pay a deposit: hold the date for 48 hours only, in writing. After 48 hours, release the date. Do not spend money on a job that has no deposit.

6. Confirming Bookings â Written Agreement or Deposit Receipt

A booking exists only when money has changed hands and a receipt has been issued. Your receipt must contain:

  • Your business name, phone, and physical address
  • Client name and phone number
  • Event date and venue
  • Total contract value
  • Deposit received and date received
  • Balance amount and due date
  • Scope summary (one line) and reference to the signed brief
  • Cancellation policy: "Deposit is non-refundable if cancelled within 14 days of the event."
  • Signature and stamp

Issue two copies â one for the client, one for your file. Send a photo of the signed receipt to the client on WhatsApp the same day.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Consultation scheduled in writing within 24 hours of first enquiry
  • â Guest count captured as both "confirmed" and "maximum"
  • â Budget captured as both "wish" and "must-spend"
  • â Date, start time, and rain date written down
  • â Venue visited or photographed; indoor/outdoor risk assessed
  • â Cultural and religious requirements listed in the brief
  • â One-page brief signed by both parties and photographed
  • â Deposit received and receipt issued before any spending

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • ILO â Safety and Health in the Events and Entertainment Sector
  • UN World Tourism Organization â Events and Tourism Resources
  • South African Events Council â Industry Guidelines
  • Kenya Association of Hotelkeepers and Caterers â Event Services Guidance
  • U.S. SBA â Writing Contracts and Business Agreements (free templates)

Bottom line: In the African event business, the consultation is not a chat â it is a contract in the making. Capture the numbers, write the brief, take the deposit, issue the receipt. Do this every time and your business will survive the busy season and the slow one.

quiz.q: What is the first step before a client meeting?
quiz.explanation: Scheduling ensures both parties are available and prepared.

quiz.q: During a WhatsApp call consultation, what should you have ready?
quiz.explanation: Taking notes helps you remember important details.

quiz.q: Why is it important to ask about cultural requirements?
options: B) To respect traditions and avoid offense
C) To make the event longer
quiz.explanation: Cultural sensitivity is crucial for a successful event in Africa.

quiz.q: What should you do if a client is unsure about their budget?
options: A) Refuse to work with them
B) Give a range based on similar events
C) Ask for a higher deposit
quiz.explanation: Providing a range helps the client understand costs and make decisions.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a key question to ask during consultation?
quiz.explanation: While preferences matter, guest count, date, and budget are essential for planning.

quiz.q: What is an event brief?
options: A) A summary of key event details
quiz.explanation: An event brief captures all important information for planning.

quiz.q: How many copies of the event brief should you make?
quiz.explanation: One for you and one for the client ensures both have a record.

quiz.q: What should be included in the event brief?
options: B) Client details and event specifics
quiz.explanation: The brief should focus on the client and event details.

quiz.q: Why is it important to read the brief back to the client?
quiz.explanation: Confirming ensures both parties agree on the details.

quiz.q: What is a common challenge for outdoor events in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Weather conditions like rain and wind can disrupt outdoor events.

quiz.q: What should you discuss with a client planning an indoor event?
options: A) Ceiling height and power outlets
B) The color of the building
quiz.explanation: These factors affect decoration and equipment setup.

quiz.q: What is a good backup plan for an outdoor event?
options: C) Move it to a beach
quiz.explanation: A tent provides shelter in case of rain or too much sun.

quiz.q: How can you manage client expectations regarding budget?
options: B) Be honest about what is possible
quiz.explanation: Honesty builds trust and prevents disappointment.

quiz.q: What is a polite way to handle a client who wants changes after the brief is signed?
options: B) Explain the cost and timeline impact
quiz.explanation: Explaining helps the client understand the consequences of changes.

quiz.q: What should you do if a client becomes abusive?
quiz.explanation: Ending the conversation maintains professionalism and safety.

quiz.q: Why should you document changes in writing?
quiz.explanation: Written records prevent misunderstandings and disputes.

quiz.q: What is a win-win solution in negotiation?
options: A) You get everything you want
quiz.explanation: A win-win solution benefits both you and the client.

quiz.q: What should be included in a booking agreement?
quiz.explanation: These details are essential for a clear agreement.

quiz.q: What is a common deposit amount for event services?
quiz.explanation: A deposit of 50-70% is common to secure bookings.

quiz.q: Why is a written agreement important in Africa?
options: C) It is required by law
quiz.explanation: It provides legal protection and clarity.

quiz.q: What should you do after receiving a deposit?
quiz.explanation: A receipt confirms payment and serves as proof.

quiz.q: How can you send an agreement to a client who is far?
quiz.explanation: WhatsApp is a common and fast method in Africa.

quiz.q: What is a cancellation policy?
quiz.explanation: It states what happens if the event is cancelled.

quiz.q: What should you do if a client wants a lavish outdoor wedding but has a small budget?
quiz.explanation: Offering alternatives helps meet their vision within budget.

quiz.q: What is a key element of a simple event brief?
quiz.explanation: Date and venue are fundamental details.

quiz.q: Why is it important to confirm the next steps after a consultation?
options: A) To keep the client informed
quiz.explanation: It ensures both parties know what to do next.

quiz.q: What is a common tool for taking notes during a consultation?
quiz.explanation: Simple tools are effective for recording details.

quiz.q: What should you do if a client is indecisive?
options: B) Offer suggestions based on experience
quiz.explanation: Guiding them helps move the planning forward.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of using a receipt book?
options: A) It is cheap and organized
quiz.explanation: Receipt books are affordable and provide a professional record.

quiz.q: What should you do if a client asks for a discount?
options: B) Explain your value and offer alternatives
quiz.explanation: Communicating value helps maintain your rates while addressing concerns.
